title: Cuticular morphology and wax attachment in New Zealand Zopheridae (Coleoptera)
content:
Abstract
Camouflage is a critical survival strategy that enables organisms to avoid detection by others. Although colour-based camouflage has been studied extensively, debris cloaking, a strategy whereby animals actively or passively collect environmental material, remains poorly understood. Beetles of the family Zopheridae, particularly diverse in the New Zealand fauna, offer a valuable model for investigating the debris cloaking phenomenon owing to their various morphologies, including adhesive secretions and/or varied elytral microstructures, which are involved in cloaking. In this study, we examine the elytral surface morphology of 17 Zopheridae species using scanning electron microscopy and confocal laser scanning microscopy. We describe three functional classes of setae: sensory setae, guard acanthae that protect sensilla from clogging, and trap setae that enhance the adhesion of environmental debris. Our results reveal a passive debris cloaking mechanism, in which fluid secretions and specialized microstructures work in concert to retain wax, debris, and microbial epibionts on the cuticle. This cloaking is likely to serve multiple adaptive functions, including camouflage, mechanical protection, and potential ecological interactions with surface-dwelling microorganisms. These findings provide new insight into the biomechanical and evolutionary basis of debris cloaking and establish Zopheridae beetles as a compelling system for studying non-visual camouflage strategies.
